illustration.alt: Amazon, wearing a fake mustache at its own ad auction, holds a $9.50 soft-reserve card while a $9 advertiser receives the sponsored paper-towel placement and a $9 bill.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Amazon ranked sponsored ads using relevance and bid size, then applied hard and soft reserve prices. When a relevant winner exceeded the hard reserve but fell below the soft reserve, it received the placement and paid its own bid instead of one cent above the next outside bid.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Amazon can be pictured entering its own auction in a fake mustache, placing a soft-reserve bid that makes the outside winner pay much more—or even pay its own bid—while the auction is still described as second-price.

preschool.title: Amazon’s Mustache Bid
preschool.lesson: Amazon’s soft reserve could make a relevant advertiser pay its own maximum bid rather than one cent above the next outside bid, which the FTC alleges made a supposed second-price auction operate like a first-price auction.
paragraphs:
On Amazon, sellers bid to appear
When shoppers search for paper towels or gear.
A “sponsored” result is an ad in the race,
And relevance helps it win the prized space.

In a second-price auction, the highest bid wins,
But the runner-up’s price is where payment begins.
With bids of $10, $8, and $6 in the fight,
The winner pays $8.01—not ten outright.

Yet relevant ads drew a much smaller crowd,
So second-best offers were not very loud.
Amazon thought premium spaces sold low,
And added a “soft reserve” to the show.

Imagine Amazon bidding in a mustache disguise,
With “true market value” machine-learning supplies.
If bidders offered $10, $2, and $1.50 that day,
A $9.50 reserve made the winner pay $9.50.

But suppose the best outside offer was $9,
While Amazon’s soft reserve stood at $9.50.
Amazon would not keep its own advertising space;
The $9 bidder won—and paid $9 for the place.

“Good news, you won! Now pay your full bid!”
That sounds like first-price, whatever the label said.
The FTC and 22 states sued Amazon, declaring
That its hidden surcharge made second-price billing misleading.

Amazon disagreed: reserves are common, it said,
And automated tools judge results instead.
In 2024, relevance often ruled the amount:
About 92% of selected ads were not the top bid by count.

What happened? The FTC alleges that Amazon’s undisclosed soft reserves caused Sponsored Products advertisers to pay their own bids close to 80% of the time, despite descriptions of a second-price auction. Amazon says its reserves reflect placement value and advertisers optimize automated bids using actual results.

illustration.alt: Markiplier holds a block representing 13.5 million GoPro shares as Lucas Shaw’s Bloomberg newsletter sends GoPro’s price upward, while a Starman Optical merger agreement arrives the next morning.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Markiplier’s previously disclosed large stake was newly noticed, helping produce a meme-stock rally and possible short-squeeze buying just before GoPro announced a cash-and-stock merger that had likely been negotiated earlier.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: GoPro became a meme stock on Monday and announced a sale of nearly the entire company on Tuesday—an unusually literal and extremely fast version of the meme-stock playbook of selling stock while the price is hot.

preschool.title: GoPro’s Monday Zoom and Tuesday Deal
preschool.lesson: A newly noticed celebrity stake helped trigger a meme-stock rally, but GoPro immediately announced a previously negotiated cash-and-stock merger before excited traders could push expectations beyond what its buyer would pay.
paragraphs:
GoPro made cameras for action and flight,
But its battered stock was a sorrowful sight.
At sixty cents each, all its shares in the land
Were worth about $110 million combined.

By early July, YouTube star Mark Fischbach—Markiplier—
Had bought 13.5 million shares as a buyer.
That was 8.5% of GoPro, a sizable collection;
He filed with the SEC on August 20, to little reaction.

Then Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw spread the word:
“Markiplier is GoPro’s largest shareholder!” readers heard.
Old news suddenly felt fresh, and the buyers poured in;
Monday’s price leaped 46%—a meme-stock spin.

Some traders had “shorted,” betting GoPro would fall.
A jump can make them buy shares back after all.
That scramble, called a short squeeze, can lift prices higher,
Especially when a famous new owner excites every buyer.

But Tuesday brought news with astonishing speed:
GoPro and Starman Optical had already agreed.
Starman would pay shareholders $285 million in cash—
About $1.14 per share—while they kept a 10% stash.

The deal had surely been brewing before Monday’s surprise,
Yet the sudden meme rally made expectations rise.
If traders dreamed of ten dollars while Starman would not,
Finishing quickly became rather urgent on the spot.

What happened? After a Bloomberg newsletter highlighted Mark Fischbach’s previously disclosed 8.5% GoPro stake, the stock jumped 46% on Monday. On Tuesday, GoPro announced its already-negotiated merger with Starman Optical, offering $1.14 cash per share, continued 10% ownership, and repayment of about $92 million in debt.

illustration.alt: A Kalshi spokesperson asks puzzled state gambling regulators for a self-exclusion list while holding a federal financial-market document, as Bloomberg reporter Ira Boudway takes notes.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Kalshi offers event contracts as a federally regulated financial market, which probably exempts it from state gambling regulations focused on addiction and consumer protection; it voluntarily offers controls such as deposit limits and self-exclusion and has requested state self-exclusion lists.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Kalshi tells states that it is not subject to their gambling rules, then asks those same states to help it act like a responsible gambling site by sharing their lists of self-excluded gamblers.

preschool.title: Kalshi’s Curious List
preschool.lesson: Because Kalshi is federally regulated as a financial market, it is probably exempt from state gambling protections, even while voluntarily seeking state self-exclusion lists to reduce gambling harm.
paragraphs:
Bloomberg’s Ira Boudway reported one case:
A gambler in Utah had slipped from a safer place.
After quitting, the person returned through Kalshi’s door,
Trading event contracts—and gambling once more.

Kalshi called it “a cherry-picked case,”
But a bigger, stranger puzzle was taking place.
People trade on events—will they happen or not?
Their contracts gain or lose depending on the result they’ve got.

Kalshi looks like online betting at play,
Yet federal rules treat it as a financial market today.
Federal watchdogs check whether trades have been swayed
By fraud, inside information, or tricks people played.

State gambling officers focus elsewhere:
On addiction, age limits, and keeping users in their care.
Yet Kalshi permits trading at eighteen years old,
Even in Utah, where gambling is not allowed.

Kalshi lets users pause, cap deposits, or choose
Self-exclusion: “Lock me out, so I cannot lose.”
With treatment providers and the National Council on Problem Gambling,
It tries to curb harmful behavior before losses keep tumbling.

Then Kalshi asked state regulators to share every name
Of people who had barred themselves from the gambling game.
Yet Kalshi says those states’ gambling rules don’t apply—
So the lists have not arrived, and it’s easy to see why.

What happened? An unnamed Utah gambling addict reportedly relapsed by trading event contracts on Kalshi. Kalshi is federally regulated as a financial market and probably exempt from state gambling rules, but it still asked state regulators for their lists of people who had chosen to be excluded from gambling.
